claim: Mindset-achievement correlations are small but positive and recur across large samples (r about .10 in the Sisk meta-analysis of 273 effects; r=.24 with high-school grades in three large studies, N=23,446, and r=.27 to .34 with test scores in California CORE and Chile datasets reported by proponents; PISA 2018 test scores positive in 72 of 74 nations). Correlational, so causation is not shown.
agent_test: Not directly testable: an LLM has no stable mindset trait (c24).
audit_note: Sisk (k=273, r=.10) and PISA 72 of 74 match, but in Yeager et al. only r=.24 (three studies, N=23,446) is with grades; r=.27-.28 (California CORE) and .34 (Chile) are with test scores, so 'r .24-.34 with grades' is mislabelled; PISA is also test scores.
claim_before_audit: Mindset-achievement correlations are small but positive and recur across large samples (r about .10 in the Sisk meta-analysis of 273 effects; r .24-.34 with grades in big proponent-led datasets; PISA 2018 positive in 72 of 74 nations). Correlational, so causation is not shown.

claim: Student-level growth mindset interventions give a small average gain on achievement: d=0.05 (Macnamara and Burgoyne, 63 studies) versus 0.09 SD (Tipton/Yeager re-analysis; 0.05 after their corrections). The sceptics find 0.02 and non-significant in the highest-quality subset.
agent_test: Use as the prior for any belief-style prompt: expect about a tenth of a SD at best.

claim: The one pre-registered national RCT (NSLM, 12,490 students, 65 schools) found +0.10 grade points (d=0.11) for lower achievers and about 0 (0.01) for higher achievers; run by proponents.
agent_test: Treat as a targeted-subgroup effect: test prompts only on items the agent finds hard, against the same items without the prompt.

claim: The effect depends on context: bigger in schools with challenge-seeking peer norms (B=0.11) and with growth-mindset teachers (CATE .11 versus -.02 for fixed-mindset teachers). Intervention without a supportive environment does little. Both findings come from the same proponent team and dataset. Gap search: an independent Chile census study (292,960 students, 24,636 teachers) finds teacher growth mindset adds only +0.02 SD, larger in low-income schools (d14); a Psychological Science teacher-delivered trial reportedly found larger gains for students of fixed-mindset teachers, the reverse direction (d17, snippet only).
agent_test: Test a belief-style prompt with and without an environment that rewards revision (verifier feedback, retry allowed) at equal tokens.

claim: Heterogeneity is large: 95% prediction interval -0.22 to 0.40 (Tipton) or -0.08 to 0.35 (Burnette); some contexts show zero or negative effect. Scale-up effects shrink (Opower example).
agent_test: Report per-item variance of any prompt effect, not only the mean.
audit_note: Numbers match (prediction intervals -0.22 to 0.40 and -0.08 to 0.35; Opower 17 experiments, 600,000 then 8 million households), but both intervals come from the single Tipton et al. 2023 paper (listed four times; Burnette's interval is quoted inside it), and the second source, Bryan, Tipton and Yeager 2021, is by overlapping authors from the same heterogeneity-advocacy group.

claim: Mindset manipulations changed the targeted belief strongly (d=0.33 in NSLM, d=0.37 in the teacher study) while grades moved little, so belief change and outcome change are weakly coupled.
agent_test: Check that a persona or mindset prompt changes agent behaviour (more retries, more revisions) before expecting an accuracy change.
audit_note: d=0.33 and d=0.37 are both manipulation checks in the same National Study of Learning Mindsets by the same lab (not two experiments); also d=0.33 is small-to-moderate rather than 'strong', and the 'weak coupling' reading is an inference (grades rose 0.10 points for lower achievers, 0.11 SD in growth-mindset teachers' classes).

claim: The mindset and error-monitoring mechanism claim (Moser 2011) failed to replicate: N=89, interaction in the wrong direction, post-error accuracy r=.04.
agent_test: Do not build an error-monitoring operator on the claim that mindset changes error response.

claim: Independent tests of mindset ideas are null or weak. EEF Changing Mindsets RCT: 101 schools, 5,018 pupils, KS2 maths effect -0.01 (CI -0.04 to 0.01), reading -0.00, 0 months (d13, read). Li and Bates 2020: n=832, mindset-grades beta -0.02 and -0.05 (d12, read). Praise: Mueller and Dweck Study 3 verified (38% vs 13% vs 14% misreported scores, N=88, d09) but a China replication (N=103) supports only the ability-praise harm, not the effort-praise benefit (d10).
agent_test: Not applicable directly; caution against importing the Mueller-Dweck praise result as a design rule.
audit_note: EEF (101 schools, 5,018 pupils, maths -0.01 CI -0.04 to 0.01), Li and Bates 2020 (n=832, beta -0.02 and -0.05), Mueller and Dweck Study 3 (N=88, 38/13/14%) and Zhao et al. (N=103, partial support, effort praise raised test anxiety vs no praise) all match; Mueller and Dweck is the original authors' own study so it is a verification, not an independent test.

claim: Extrinsic rewards undermine intrinsic motivation for engagement-, completion- and performance-contingent rewards (free-choice d -0.40, -0.36, -0.28), while positive feedback raises it (d +0.33). Disputes in the literature not examined here.
agent_test: Not testable on a model: no intrinsic motivation. Only analog is feedback framing in the loop (verbal critique versus bare score).

claim: Emotional or importance stimuli raised average benchmark scores in the original EmotionPrompt paper (+8.00% relative on Instruction Induction, +115% on BIG-Bench), but GPT-4 zero-shot average was lower than baseline (78.96 vs 80.75) and gain varies by model. All from one group. Gap search: a pre-specified 28,000-trial test on five 2026 models found both positive and negative framing about 1.3-1.4 pp below neutral (Holm p about .06) and states the original claim rests on 13-20 items (d05); a six-benchmark study found only small changes (d04). Gains do not carry to current models.
agent_test: Run an EP02-style sentence versus none at equal tokens across 3+ models and 5+ seeds, with variance.

claim: Negative-emotion prompts also raised scores in NegativePrompt (+12.89% relative on Instruction Induction, +46.25% on BIG-Bench; older models), which hints that the lift may come from any salient addition rather than psychology-specific content (inference, not tested). A 2026 workshop poster (five unnamed frontier models, four reasoning benchmarks, 28,000 trials) found positive minus negative framing +0.04 pp (CI -0.34 to +0.42) and both framings slightly below neutral (-1.3 to -1.4 pp, not significant after Holm correction), so valence made no detectable difference there and the lift does not carry over to those models.
agent_test: Compare positive, negative and length-matched neutral sentences; if all lift equally, drop the psychological reading.
audit_note: NegativePrompt numbers (12.89%, 46.25%, 45 tasks, 5 models) and the +0.04 pp [-0.34, +0.42] result match, but the same 2026 poster found both emotional framings 1.3-1.4 pp below neutral (Holm p about .06), which cuts against 'any salient addition lifts scores', and 'valence does not matter on current models' generalises one unreviewed workshop poster on five unnamed models and four reasoning benchmarks.
claim_before_audit: Negative-emotion prompts also raised scores (+12.89% Instruction Induction, +46.25% BIG-Bench), which hints that the lift comes from any salient addition, not psychology-specific content. Inference, not tested. Gap search: positive minus negative was +0.04 pp (CI -0.34 to +0.42), so valence does not matter on current models (d05).

claim: A large controlled test found tipping and threats have no significant aggregate effect on GPQA (N=4,950) and MMLU-Pro (N=2,500), though per-question effects reach +36 and -35 points. The report covered 5 models including the reasoning model o4-mini (25 trials per question): only 5 of GPQA comparisons and 10 of MMLU-Pro comparisons differed from baseline, uncorrected (d01).
agent_test: Treat any motivational sentence as noise unless it beats a control on held-out items with per-question variance reported.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-20 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Politeness effects depend on model and language: rudest prompts hurt GPT-3.5 (51.93 vs 57-60) and Llama2-70B (28.44 vs 49-55) but not GPT-4 (73.9-79.1); a 250-prompt GPT-4o study found rude prompts scored higher (84.8 vs 80.8).
agent_test: Tone is not worth a schema slot; fix one neutral tone.

claim: Role personas in system prompts do not reliably help: the best persona per question helps only if known in advance; automatic choice is near random (162 roles, 2,410 MMLU questions). Gap search: Prompting Science Report 4 (6 models incl. o3-mini and o4-mini; 198 GPQA and 300 MMLU-Pro questions; 25 runs each) finds no consistent expert-persona gain and harm from low-knowledge personas (d03).
agent_test: Do not add a persona operator; consistent with SCHEMA section 4b.
audit_note: Zheng et al. (162 roles, 2,410 questions drawn from MMLU, 4 model families, selection near random) and Prompting Science Report 4 (6 models, GPQA Diamond 198 and MMLU-Pro 300 questions, 25 runs, no consistent expert gain, low-knowledge personas often hurt) match.

claim: Auto-optimised phrasings matter: 'Take a deep breath and work on this problem step-by-step' got 80.2 on GSM8K versus 71.8 for 'Let's think step by step' and 34.0 with no instruction (PaLM 2-L); optimizer- and model-specific.
agent_test: Wording is model-specific; any wording must be tuned per model on dev data.

claim: Trust-framed system prompts raised hidden-issue discovery in agent debugging (+59%, d=2.28, 9 scenarios; +25% in 135 automated points) while fear framing did nothing. Single author, one model, small N, framing tied to a named methodology.
agent_test: Replicate on 50+ scenarios, 3 models, with a length-matched neutral control at equal token budget.

claim: Intrinsic self-correction without external feedback does not help and often hurts (GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 89.0; GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 41.8), so an encouragement-style 'you can improve, try again' prompt is not expected to work without a verifier signal; Reflexion loops with feedback do help (HumanEval 91 vs 80). Gap search: Kamoi 2024 survey finds no fair-setting success for prompted self-feedback and that positive results used oracle information (d08). A direct verifier-by-encouragement 2x2 still does not exist.
agent_test: Compare retry-with-verifier, retry-with-encouragement and single shot at equal tokens.
audit_note: Huang (GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 89.0; GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 41.8), Shinn (HumanEval 91% vs GPT-4 80%) and Kamoi (abstract: no fair-setting prompted self-correction success; oracle/unfair settings table) match; the encouragement-prompt expectation and the 'no 2x2 exists' statement are inferences/absence claims, and Reflexion's HumanEval gain uses self-generated test feedback, whereas Kamoi flags some Reflexion tasks as oracle-based.

claim: LLM-generated growth-mindset-supportive teacher language is rated better by students than expert-teacher rewrites (1,006 raters, 174 teachers; challenge-seeking choice almost doubled), but these are perceptions, not learning outcomes.
agent_test: Not an agent-thinking result; it is a use of LLMs on the human side.

claim: Unguarded LLM assistance harms later learning (GPT Base students -17% versus controls after access was removed) whereas a structured tutor prevented it; structured AI tutoring beat in-class active learning (0.63 SD, N=194). Bastani seen only in snippet.
agent_test: Not an agent test. Analog: scaffold structure matters more than raw model access.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-20 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Learned interestingness or progress signals help artificial agents (OMNI, Motif, Voyager: random curriculum drops items found by 93%), but this is exploration design, not mindset. Gap search: curiosity bonus in RLVR training gives about +2.4 average (48.2 to 50.6) on Qwen3-4B-Base (d15); no study found using curiosity or learning progress to select branches in an inference-time scaffold (d16, not opened).
agent_test: Test a curiosity-ranked task or branch selector versus random at equal tokens on a long-horizon task.
audit_note: Voyager (random curriculum drops item count by 93%), CDE (Qwen3-4B-Base GRPO 48.2, about +2.4 average) and OMNI (outperforms uniform-sampling and learning-progress baselines) match; the 'not mindset' framing and the absence of an inference-time curiosity scaffold (d16, unopened) are the author's inference.

claim: No study was found that measures growth mindset as a trait of an LLM or tests mindset-intervention-style prompts as the theory defines them (negative search result, about 25 candidates).
agent_test: Gap: a one-off test telling a model that ability is malleable versus fixed, with failures in context.

claim: Mueller and Dweck 1998 numbers verified from the paper: Study 1 (123 children) performance goal choice 67% after intelligence praise vs 8% after effort praise; post-failure score change -0.92 vs +1.21 vs +0.13 control; Study 3 (N=88) misreported score 38% vs 13% vs 14%.
agent_test: None; do not map ability praise to a prompt. Kept as the founding effect size for the reader.

claim: A step-by-step scaffold prompt raises mean accuracy for older non-reasoning models (RD 0.044 to 0.135 on GPQA Diamond) but lowers the all-25-trials-correct rate for several (RD down to -0.172); for reasoning models the gain is about 0.03 or negative (Flash 2.5 -0.033). So a scaffold can raise the mean while lowering reliability.
agent_test: For any scaffold or motivational prompt, report mean accuracy and the all-trials-correct rate, on non-reasoning and reasoning models separately. Partial answer to the Bastani-style harm question (gap 8): in-loop mean gain with reliability loss.

claim: The 2x2 test of encouragement by verifier signal has not been run. Indirect evidence says encouragement without a verifier does not help (Kamoi survey), and 'positive thinking' system messages vary by model and CoT (Battle and Gollapudi, 60 snippets, 3 models, GSM8K subsets).
agent_test: Run verifier on/off x encouragement/length-matched neutral/none x 3+ models x 5+ seeds at equal tokens; this is the decision test for gaps 1 and 2.

claim: Blackwell 2007 Study 2 had 48 treated vs 43 control seventh graders (abstract); Study 1 had 373. The Study 1 association did not reappear in two near-replications (n=832; beta -0.02 and -0.05, Li and Bates 2020).
agent_test: Not applicable. Grade slopes and effect sizes of Blackwell Study 2 still unread.
audit_note: Blackwell abstract (Study 1 N=373; Study 2 N=48 vs 43) and Li and Bates (n=832; beta -0.02 and -0.05) match; Li and Bates call them near-replications but they used university undergraduates and grades across a different transition, not seventh graders.
